stories.headline: You're running an app now
stories.hook: This whole feed is three files and a database.
stories.body: High Frequency is a static web app backed by Supabase: stories live in Postgres, likes are counted globally, and the feed updates the moment a row changes.
stories.deep_dive: The card you're reading came from stories.json bundled with the app — the offline fallback. When Supabase is configured, stories load straight from the database: add a row, set published to true, and it appears in the feed instantly with no deploy. Every heart on every phone updates the same global like counter. To make this feed yours, run supabase-setup.sql in a free Supabase project and drop your keys into CONFIG at the top of app.js.

stories.headline: Why compounding feels slow then sudden
stories.hook: The curve is flat for years, then it isn't.
stories.body: Compound growth is exponential, but humans read the early, flat part as failure. Most of the payoff lives in the final stretch of the curve.
stories.deep_dive: At 10% a year, money doubles roughly every seven years. The first double is quiet; the fourth double is enormous, because each new gain is calculated on a much larger base. The practical lesson isn't about a specific asset, it's about time horizon: the people who capture exponential returns are usually the ones who simply stayed in long enough to reach the steep part of the curve.

stories.headline: How a bill actually becomes law
stories.hook: The version you hear about is rarely the one that passes.
stories.body: Legislation is a negotiation, not an announcement. A bill is introduced, reshaped in committee, amended on the floor, reconciled between chambers, then signed or vetoed.
stories.deep_dive: Most bills die quietly in committee, never reaching a vote. The ones that survive are usually amended heavily to win enough support, which is why the final text can look very different from the headline proposal. Reconciliation between two chambers is where a lot of the real bargaining happens, often out of public view. Watching what gets stripped out is frequently more informative than watching what gets announced.

stories.headline: The web is quietly getting native
stories.hook: Installable apps, offline, push — no app store required.
stories.body: Progressive Web Apps let a website install to your home screen, run full-screen, and work offline. This feed is one of them.
stories.deep_dive: A PWA is just a website that ships a manifest describing how it should install, plus a service worker that caches its files. That combination is enough for the browser to offer 'Add to Home Screen' and to launch the site full-screen with its own icon. The upside is reach without an app store; the tradeoff is that some deep native APIs remain restricted. For a content feed like this one, the web platform is more than enough.

stories.headline: Inflation is a tax nobody voted for
stories.hook: When prices rise, idle cash quietly loses value.
stories.body: Inflation erodes purchasing power. Money sitting still buys a little less each year, which is why 'safe' cash isn't risk-free.
stories.deep_dive: At 3% annual inflation, cash loses roughly a quarter of its purchasing power over a decade. That's the hidden cost of holding everything in currency: you feel safe because the number on the account doesn't drop, but what that number can buy does. This is the core argument for owning productive assets over time, and the reason central banks watch inflation so closely — it reshapes every saving and borrowing decision in the economy.

stories.headline: Turnout decides more than opinion
stories.hook: Elections often turn on who shows up, not who's persuaded.
stories.body: Campaigns spend enormous effort not on changing minds but on getting existing supporters to actually vote.
stories.deep_dive: Persuasion is expensive and slow; mobilization is cheaper and faster. In many races the pool of truly undecided voters is small, so the marginal vote is easier to win by activating a supporter who might have stayed home than by converting an opponent. That's why so much political money flows into registration drives, reminders, and reducing the friction of voting. Understanding this reframes a lot of political news: watch the turnout machinery, not just the polls.
